---
title: "Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors"
---

This appendix describes the SBayesRC-style annotation-dependent BayesR prior
available through `stblr_csr_annot(annotation_model = "sbayesrc")` and the
compatibility wrapper `stblr_csr_annot(..., annotation_model = "sbayesrc")`. The core prior family is
closely aligned with published SBayesRC: marker effects follow a multi-normal
mixture, and marker-specific mixture probabilities are determined by
conditional probit stick-breaking regressions on annotations. The exposed
`sblr` model is not an exact reproduction of the published GCTB SBayesRC
implementation. Its default gamma grid differs, and it uses a CSR sparse-LD
likelihood rather than the GCTB low-rank rotated summary-statistics likelihood.

This note focuses on the annotation-dependent prior and its diagnostics. It
does not claim computational equivalence between the two likelihood
implementations.

## Model Definition

For marker $i$, let $z_i \in \{1,\ldots,C\}$ identify one of $C$ mixture
components. Conditional on $z_i=k$, the marker effect is

$$
\beta_i \mid z_i=k, v_b, \gamma
\sim
N(0,\gamma_k v_b).
$$

The vector

$$
\gamma=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_C)
$$

contains fixed variance multipliers, while $v_b$ is the sampled global
active-effect variance scale. The implementation requires

$$
\gamma_1=0,
\qquad
\gamma_k>0 \quad \text{for } k>1.
$$

The first component is therefore an exact null component:

$$
\beta_i=0 \quad \text{when } z_i=1.
$$

The remaining components represent increasingly diffuse active-effect
distributions when their gamma multipliers increase.

For multiple traits supplied to the wrapper, this mixture construction and its
annotation coefficients are fitted separately by trait. The formatted fit
therefore stores one `alpha` matrix and one set of marker component summaries
per trait.

## Optional BayesS-Style `selection_s`

The package argument is `selection_s`. It corresponds to the BayesS-style MAF
architecture parameter `S`.

Current CSR SBayesRC supports both fixed global `selection_s` and sampled
trait-specific `selection_s` by Metropolis-Hastings. SBayesRC annotations and
`selection_s` affect different parts of the prior:

- annotations affect marker-specific component probabilities through
  $A\alpha$ and probit stick-breaking;
- `selection_s` affects marker-specific effect-size prior variance.

CSR effects are on the standardized-genotype scale. The MAF-dependent prior
scale is

$$
q_j(S)=h_j^{S+1},
\qquad
h_j=2p_j(1-p_j),
$$

where $p_j$ is the minor allele frequency. The `+1` exponent is used because
the CSR sampler effects are standardized-genotype-scale effects rather than
allele-scale effects.

With fixed `selection_s`, the active SBayesRC component prior is

$$
b_j \mid \mathrm{component}_j=m,v_b,S
\sim
N\{0, v_b\gamma_m q_j(S)\}.
$$

With sampled `selection_s`, the current implementation samples one $S_t$ per
trait and chain using the active-component MH log posterior contribution

```text
log p(S_t | b_t, gamma_t, vb_t)
  = log p(S_t)
    - 0.5 sum_{j: gamma_jt > 0} [
        log q_j(S_t) + b_jt^2 / (vb_t gamma_jt q_j(S_t))
      ]
```

The sampled-S defaults are:

```r
selection_s_init = 0
selection_s_prior = c(-3, 2)
selection_s_proposal_sd = 0.35
```

The same fixed and sampled `selection_s` support is available for plain CSR
BayesC and plain CSR BayesR. Scheduled CSR BayesC, BayesC-like
annotation-aware CSR backends, and BED backends do not support sampler-level
`selection_s`. See [selection_s implementation status](selection_s_status.md)
for the complete backend support matrix and BayesC/BayesR kernels.

## Gamma Grids

The public `sblr` default is:

```r
gamma = c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
```

Published SBayesRC uses the five-component grid:

```r
gamma = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
```

Users can request that published gamma grid explicitly:

```r
fit <- stblr_csr_annot(
  stats = stats,
  Glist = Glist,
  annotations = A,
  annotation_model = "sbayesrc",
  gamma = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
)
```

Matching the gamma grid aligns this part of the prior specification. It does
not make the complete `sblr` model identical to GCTB SBayesRC because the
likelihood, sparse-LD representation, exposed defaults, and implementation
details remain distinct.

## Annotation-Dependent Component Probabilities

Let $A$ be an $m \times K$ marker-by-annotation matrix. For $C$ mixture
components, let $\alpha$ be a $K \times (C-1)$ coefficient matrix. Column
$\alpha_j$ controls conditional stick-breaking step $j$.

For marker $i$ and step $j$, the linear predictor and conditional
continuation probability are

$$
\eta_{ij}=A_i\alpha_j,
\qquad
p_{ij}=\Phi(\eta_{ij}),
$$

where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. The marker-level
component probabilities are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{i1} &= 1-p_{i1},\\
\pi_{i2} &= p_{i1}(1-p_{i2}),\\
\pi_{i3} &= p_{i1}p_{i2}(1-p_{i3}),\\
&\ \vdots\\
\pi_{iC} &= \prod_{j=1}^{C-1}p_{ij}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, component $k<C$ receives the probability of continuing through
all earlier steps and stopping at step $k$; the final component receives the
probability of continuing through every step.

### Why the probabilities sum to one

For a marker with step probabilities $p_1,\ldots,p_{C-1}$,

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{C}\pi_k
=
(1-p_1)
+p_1(1-p_2)
+\cdots+
\left(\prod_{j=1}^{C-2}p_j\right)(1-p_{C-1})
+\prod_{j=1}^{C-1}p_j
=1.
$$

The expression telescopes: probability either stops at one of the first
$C-1$ steps or reaches the final component.

### Numerical flooring and renormalization

The native sampler computes these probabilities from $A\alpha$, floors each
component probability at `pi_floor`, and renormalizes each marker row to sum to
one. The public default is `pi_floor = 1e-12`.

Flooring prevents exact numerical zero probabilities when probit predictors are
extreme. Because flooring slightly changes the unnormalized stick-breaking
probabilities, the subsequent row renormalization is required. This is a
numerical-stability adjustment, not a different conceptual link function.

The deterministic R diagnostic helpers apply the mathematical
stick-breaking transform without the native sampler's floor-and-renormalize
step. For ordinary finite coefficients, their rows sum to one up to numerical
tolerance.

## Annotation Matrix and Preprocessing

Rows of $A$ must be aligned with the markers in the sufficient statistics,
CSR sparse-LD matrix, and posterior outputs. Columns may contain binary or
quantitative annotations, and overlap is allowed.

Before fitting, `stblr_csr_annot(..., annotation_model = "sbayesrc")` calls the shared annotation
preparation helper using these controls:

- `add_intercept = TRUE` adds an all-ones first column when one is not already
  recognized;
- `standardize_annotations = TRUE` centers and scales nonbinary quantitative
  annotations;
- `center_binary_annotations = FALSE` leaves binary columns unchanged by
  default;
- row names can be used to reorder $A$ to known marker names when all names
  are available.

The preprocessing choices determine the meaning and scale of `alpha`.
Quantitative coefficients are effects per standardized annotation unit under
the defaults. An unchanged binary coefficient is a contrast associated with
membership in that annotation, conditional on the remaining columns.

### Intercept prior

With `intercept_flat = TRUE`, the first annotation coefficient at every
stick-breaking step receives a flat prior in the native alpha update. This
assumes the first column is the intercept, which is the arrangement produced
when the wrapper adds it. All other annotation coefficients receive the
normal prior described below.

If a custom matrix already contains an intercept, place it first when relying
on `intercept_flat = TRUE`. An all-ones column elsewhere in the matrix is not
treated as the flat-prior intercept by the native update.

## Alpha and SigmaSqAlpha Priors

For non-intercept annotation coefficient $k$ at stick-breaking step $j$,
the implemented prior is

$$
\alpha_{kj}\mid \sigma_{\alpha,j}^2
\sim
N(0,\sigma_{\alpha,j}^2).
$$

Each step has its own annotation-effect variance
$\sigma_{\alpha,j}^2$, represented by `sigmaSqAlpha[j]`. Under
`intercept_flat = TRUE`, the first coefficient is excluded from this normal
shrinkage prior and from the variance update.

The variance update has scaled-inverse-chi-square or inverse-gamma family form:

$$
\sigma_{\alpha,j}^2
=
\frac{
\sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}}\alpha_{kj}^2 + b_\alpha
}{
\chi^2_{|\mathcal{R}|+a_\alpha}
},
$$

where $\mathcal{R}$ contains coefficients subject to shrinkage,
`sigmaSqAlpha_a` supplies $a_\alpha$, and `sigmaSqAlpha_b` supplies
$b_\alpha$. Both public defaults are 2.

This construction is aligned with the published SBayesRC use of normal
annotation-coefficient priors and a scaled-inverse-chi-square-family variance
prior. The exact published hyperparameter specification should not be inferred
from the `sblr` defaults. Users should report the values supplied to
`sigmaSqAlpha_a`, `sigmaSqAlpha_b`, `sigmaSqAlpha_init`, and
`intercept_flat`.

## Gibbs-Style Alpha Updating

When `updateAlpha = TRUE`, the native sampler updates alpha every
`alpha_update_every` iterations. The public default interval is 10.

The update uses conditional probit data augmentation. At stick-breaking step
$j$, only markers that reached that step are included. A latent normal
variable is sampled for each eligible marker:

$$
\ell_{ij}\mid \alpha_j
\sim
N(A_i\alpha_j,1),
$$

truncated above zero when the marker continues beyond step $j$, and truncated
at or below zero when it stops at that step.

Conditional on the latent variables and the other coefficients, each
annotation coefficient has a normal full conditional. For a non-intercept
coefficient, the prior precision $1/\sigma_{\alpha,j}^2$ is added to the
data precision. With `intercept_flat = TRUE`, the first coefficient omits that
prior precision. After the coefficients for a step are updated,
`sigmaSqAlpha[j]` is drawn from the scaled-inverse-chi-square-family update.

This is a Gibbs-style conditional update using truncated-normal augmentation
and normal draws. It is not a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings alpha update.
After an alpha update, the native sampler recomputes all marker-specific prior
component probabilities from $A\alpha$.

## Initialization

`make_sbayesrc_alpha_init()` creates deterministic initial values for the
annotation-dependent mixture architecture.

Given an initial overall active probability `pi_init`, it distributes active
mass across the $C-1$ non-null components using normalized
`active_comp_weights`. This produces initial marginal component probabilities

$$
\pi^{(0)}
=
\left(
1-\pi_{\mathrm{init}},
\pi_{\mathrm{init}}w_2,
\ldots,
\pi_{\mathrm{init}}w_C
\right).
$$

The helper then converts these marginal probabilities to conditional
continuation probabilities for the stick-breaking representation. When $A$
contains an all-ones column, the first such column receives intercept
coefficients

$$
\alpha_{0j}^{(0)}
=
\Phi^{-1}\{p_j^{(0)}\},
$$

and all other coefficients begin at zero. If no all-ones column exists, all
default coefficients are zero. Supplied `alpha_init` and
`sigmaSqAlpha_init` values are accepted after dimension and finite-value
validation.

The helper also returns named initial component probabilities, normalized
active-component weights, conditional step probabilities, gamma values, and
component names. These make initialization auditable without running the
sampler.

## Marker-Effect and Component Updates

For each marker, the sampler combines the annotation-derived prior component
probabilities with the summary-statistics likelihood. The exact null component
has $\gamma_1=0$ and leaves the marker effect at zero. For active component
$k$, the effect prior variance is

$$
v_{b,k}=\gamma_k v_b.
$$

The sampler forms a component-specific Bayes factor using the current marker
score, residual variance, marker diagonal cross-product, and $v_{b,k}$.
It samples a new component from the resulting posterior component
probabilities, then samples the marker effect from its conditional normal
distribution when the selected gamma is positive.

The global scale $v_b$ may also be updated from currently active marker
effects and their selected gamma values when `updateB = TRUE`. Thus gamma
defines relative component scales, while $v_b$ supplies the shared sampled
scale.

## Fit Outputs

The formatted fit exposes the standard marker and variance summaries together
with SBayesRC-style architecture summaries.

### `alpha`

`fit$alpha` is a list with one posterior-mean coefficient matrix per trait.
Each matrix has annotations in rows and stick-breaking steps in columns.
Because it is a posterior mean, applying a nonlinear probability transform to
it gives a plug-in diagnostic, not the posterior mean of that transformed
quantity.

### `sigmaSqAlpha`

`fit$sigmaSqAlpha` is a trait-by-step matrix of posterior mean annotation-effect
variance parameters. Large values permit more dispersion among non-intercept
annotation coefficients at that stick-breaking step. They should be
interpreted together with alpha coefficients, annotation scaling, and chain
diagnostics.

### `component_probabilities`

`fit$component_probabilities` is a list with one marker-by-component matrix per trait. It
contains posterior frequencies of sampled component assignments after burn-in
and thinning. It is not the same object as the annotation-derived prior
probability matrix computed from $A\alpha$.

Component probability columns are named by gamma values. The exact null
component column is `gamma_0.00`, so `dm = 1 - P(gamma_0.00)`. This differs
from CSR BayesR, which uses `component_0` for the null component column.

### `ncomp`

`fit$ncomp` is a trait-by-component matrix containing posterior mean counts of
markers assigned to each component. Its row sum should equal the number of
markers, subject only to numerical representation.

The usual outputs remain available when returned, including `bm`, `dm`,
variance traces, covariance summaries, current effects, and residual state.
Full marker-scale matrices should be retained for analysis rather than printed
in full.

## Diagnostic Helpers

Four deterministic exported helpers translate alpha coefficients into compact
prior-architecture diagnostics.

### Annotation-row diagnostics

`sbayesrc_annotation_pi(alpha, gamma)` applies the probit stick-breaking
transform separately to each row of `alpha`. It returns an
annotation-by-component probability matrix.

`sbayesrc_annotation_gamma_mean(alpha, gamma)` computes

$$
\overline{\gamma}_k^{\mathrm{annotation}}
=
\sum_{c=1}^{C}\pi_{kc}\gamma_c
$$

for each alpha row.

These are coefficient-row diagnostics. A binary annotation row, for example,
is evaluated as a standalone predictor row. It does not automatically include
the fitted intercept or the effects of correlated annotations. It should not
be described as the literal component probability for every marker carrying
that annotation.

### Marker-profile diagnostics

`sbayesrc_marker_pi(A, alpha, gamma)` first computes $A\alpha$, then applies
the stick-breaking transform. It returns an $m \times C$ marker-level prior
component probability matrix.

`sbayesrc_marker_gamma_mean(A, alpha, gamma)` computes the plug-in expected
gamma for each marker:

$$
\overline{\gamma}_i^{\mathrm{marker}}
=
\sum_{c=1}^{C}\pi_{ic}\gamma_c.
$$

These marker-profile helpers include the complete annotation combination in
each row of $A$. They are generally more directly relevant to the fitted
prior architecture than standalone annotation-row summaries.

```r
alpha_t <- fit$alpha[[1]]
prior_pi <- sbayesrc_marker_pi(fit$input$A, alpha_t, fit$input$gamma)
expected_gamma <- sbayesrc_marker_gamma_mean(
  fit$input$A, alpha_t, fit$input$gamma
)
```

Because these diagnostics transform posterior mean alpha coefficients, they do
not propagate the full posterior uncertainty in alpha. Compact reports can
show annotation-row expected gamma, `summary(expected_gamma)`, and the
correlation between marker expected gamma and PIP. That correlation describes
the fitted prior-posterior relationship; it is not a calibration statistic or
causal estimate.

## Interpretation of Annotation Effects

An alpha coefficient changes a conditional continuation probability at one
stick-breaking step. Its sign cannot be interpreted independently of component
ordering:

- a positive coefficient increases the probability of continuing past that
  step;
- a negative coefficient increases the probability of stopping at that step;
- the consequences for expected gamma depend on all later steps and the gamma
  grid.

Expected gamma is a useful scalar summary of prior mixture allocation, but it
compresses a complete component-probability vector. Two markers can have the
same expected gamma while assigning probability to different components.
Report component probabilities when those distinctions matter.

Annotation effects and expected-gamma differences are prior-architecture
summaries, not proof of biological causality. They can reflect LD, marker
density, annotation overlap, quantitative-annotation scaling, model
misspecification, and finite-chain behavior. Interpretation should compare
annotation-derived prior probabilities with posterior component frequencies
and assess sensitivity to preprocessing, gamma grids, sparse-LD settings, and
hyperparameters.

## Comparison With Published SBayesRC

| Published SBayesRC feature | `sblr` implementation | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| BayesR-like multi-normal marker-effect mixture | $\beta_i\mid z_i=k \sim N(0,\gamma_kv_b)$ | Same core prior family |
| Exact null component | Requires `gamma[1] == 0`; null effects are exactly zero | Same |
| Published gamma grid `c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)` | User-supplied and supported | Same when explicitly requested |
| Default gamma grid | `c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 1)` | Different exposed default |
| Marker-specific mixture probabilities from annotations | Uses $A\alpha$ for every marker | Same core structure |
| Conditional probit stick-breaking | Uses $p_{ij}=\Phi(A_i\alpha_j)$ and conditional continuation probabilities | Same core structure |
| Intercept and functional annotations | Adds an intercept by default; accepts overlapping binary or quantitative annotations | Closely aligned, with `sblr` preprocessing defaults |
| Quantitative annotation handling | Standardizes nonbinary annotations by default; leaves binary columns unchanged by default | Qualified implementation choice |
| Normal alpha priors with step-specific variance | Non-intercept coefficients use $N(0,\sigma_{\alpha,j}^2)$ | Same prior family |
| Scaled inverse-chi-square prior on alpha variance | Uses a scaled-inverse-chi-square/inverse-gamma-family update controlled by `sigmaSqAlpha_a` and `sigmaSqAlpha_b` | Same family; exact published hyperparameters not implied |
| Probit alpha update | Latent truncated-normal augmentation and conditional normal draws | Closely aligned Gibbs-style update |
| Component-probability numerical handling | Floors probabilities at `pi_floor` and renormalizes rows | Qualified numerical-stability detail |
| Summary-statistics likelihood | CSR sparse-LD likelihood | Different from GCTB low-rank rotated likelihood |

The most accurate description is therefore:

> `stblr_csr_annot(..., annotation_model = "sbayesrc")` implements an SBayesRC-style,
> annotation-dependent BayesR prior that is closely aligned with the published
> SBayesRC prior structure, fitted with the `sblr` CSR sparse-LD likelihood.

It should not be described as an exact reproduction of published GCTB
SBayesRC as exposed by default.

## Practical Validation Checklist

Before interpreting an SBayesRC-style fit:

- verify marker alignment among $A$, sufficient statistics, CSR LD, and
  posterior summaries;
- record the gamma grid and distinguish the `sblr` default from the published
  grid;
- record intercept, standardization, and binary-centering choices;
- inspect annotation prevalence, scaling, overlap, and collinearity;
- report `sigmaSqAlpha_a`, `sigmaSqAlpha_b`, `intercept_flat`, `pi_floor`, and
  `alpha_update_every`;
- check component counts, PIPs, variance traces, and chain behavior;
- distinguish annotation-derived prior probabilities from posterior component
  frequencies in `component_probabilities`;
- compare annotation-row and full marker-profile diagnostics;
- assess sensitivity to gamma, sparse-LD thresholds, annotations, and
  hyperparameters; and
- avoid causal claims from alpha coefficients or expected-gamma summaries.

annotation-dependent mixture priors.
## Shared MT extension

Phase 20 reuses the ST probit-stick order and coefficient-prior update for one
joint MT component state. It does not create trait-, pattern-, operator-, or
component-covariance-specific coefficient matrices. Global non-null pattern
probabilities form the second factor of the marker-state prior.
